title: Blunt splenic injury: non-operative management, embolisation or laparotomy

header.contentArea: Trauma: abdominal solid organ injury (emergency management viva)

NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management (published 17 February 2016)
UKHSA Green Book chapter 7 (last updated 10 January 2020)

related.why: Splenic anatomy and elective splenectomy, including vaccination before planned surgery
The primary survey that comes before this decision

brief.role: Core surgical trainee on the general surgical team
brief.scenario: Miss Lindqvist, 22, fell from her bike onto the handlebars 40 minutes ago. She has left upper quadrant pain and left shoulder tip pain. On arrival: pulse 118/min, BP 96/60 mmHg. The emergency team has started resuscitation.
brief.task: Discuss her assessment and management with the examiner.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Her physiology, not the CT grade, decides the pathway.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Picking splenectomy or embolisation from the grade alone, or sending an unresponsive patient to CT.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Is she responding to resuscitation? That decides whether she goes to CT or theatre."

grid.label: Haemorrhage resuscitation
grid.fail: Gives litres of crystalloid to normalise her blood pressure.
grid.pass: Large-bore access, bloods and crossmatch, blood products rather than crystalloid, tranexamic acid as soon as possible.
grid.high: Restrictive volume resuscitation until bleeding is controlled; no tranexamic acid beyond 3 hours after injury unless hyperfibrinolysis.

grid.label: FAST and CT
grid.fail: Uses a negative FAST to exclude splenic injury, or sends an unresponsive patient to CT.
grid.pass: Responding to resuscitation: immediate contrast CT, without FAST or other imaging delaying it.
grid.high: Knows a negative FAST does not exclude intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding; unresponsive shock with free fluid goes to theatre, not CT.

grid.label: Physiology decides the pathway
grid.fail: Chooses management from the CT grade alone.
grid.pass: Stable or stabilised, with no other reason for laparotomy: non-operative management whatever the grade.
grid.high: Only where there is intensive monitoring, interventional radiology, an available theatre and blood; otherwise operate or transfer.

grid.label: Angioembolisation
grid.fail: Takes a stable patient with a blush straight to splenectomy, or ignores the blush.
grid.pass: A contrast blush in a stable patient: angioembolisation, which may be first-line whatever the grade.
grid.high: Also considers embolisation for pseudoaneurysm, or persistent bleeding once other sources are excluded.

grid.label: Monitoring non-operative management
grid.fail: Admits to a general ward with daily bloods.
grid.pass: High dependency care, serial examination, serial haemoglobin, bed rest and immediate access to theatre.
grid.high: Close observation for the first 48 to 72 hours; repeat CT if haemoglobin falls; mechanical VTE prophylaxis now.

grid.label: Indications to operate
grid.fail: Persists with non-operative management despite instability.
grid.pass: Laparotomy for instability not responding to resuscitation, peritonitis or hollow viscus injury, or failed non-operative management.
grid.high: Failure means falling haemoglobin or ongoing transfusion despite embolisation; laparoscopic splenectomy is not recommended in a bleeding patient.

grid.label: Protection after splenectomy
grid.fail: Delays emergency splenectomy to vaccinate first, or forgets vaccination.
grid.pass: Pneumococcal, meningococcal ACWY and B, and annual influenza vaccines, antibiotic prophylaxis and patient information after splenectomy.
grid.high: Vaccinates no sooner than 14 days after splenectomy, or before discharge if follow-up may be missed.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Two litres of saline to get her blood pressure back to normal.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Her FAST is negative. Does that help?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Yes, that rules out a splenic injury.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: She stabilises. CT shows a high-grade splenic laceration. What now?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That confirms she needs a splenectomy today.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: If you managed her without surgery, where would she go?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The surgical ward, with bloods in the morning.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd repeat the CT and keep watching.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: And vaccination if she needs a splenectomy?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: She must be vaccinated before we operate.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Large-bore access, bloods and crossmatch, blood products rather than crystalloid, and tranexamic acid as soon as possible.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: She is responding, so immediate contrast CT. I wouldn't let FAST or other imaging hold that up.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: She responds. CT shows a high-grade laceration. How do you decide?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: On her physiology. If she is stable and nothing else needs a laparotomy, non-operative management, whatever the grade.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: In a stable patient I'd ask interventional radiology to embolise. That can be first-line whatever the grade.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: High dependency, with serial examination, serial haemoglobin and bed rest, and theatre available immediately.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: If she becomes unstable and doesn't respond, develops peritonitis, or non-operative management fails.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: She needs a splenectomy. What about infection?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: After surgery: pneumococcal, meningococcal ACWY and B, annual flu, antibiotic prophylaxis and information for her.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Blood products, not crystalloid, with a restrictive approach until the bleeding is controlled. Tranexamic acid now: it isn't given beyond 3 hours after injury unless there's hyperfibrinolysis.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That doesn't exclude intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding. If she were unresponsive with free fluid, she would go to theatre, not CT.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: She responds and CT shows a high-grade laceration.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Non-operative management is reasonable here because we have interventional radiology, a theatre and blood available now. Without those, I'd operate or transfer.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: There's a blush, and a small pseudoaneurysm.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Embolisation for both. I'd also embolise later if she keeps bleeding once other sources are excluded.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How long do you watch her closely?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The first 48 to 72 hours matter most. Repeat CT if her haemoglobin falls. Mechanical VTE prophylaxis now, and LMWH once bleeding has stopped.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: She drops her haemoglobin despite embolisation and needs repeated transfusion.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Non-operative management has failed: laparotomy and splenectomy. Not laparoscopic in a bleeding patient.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: No sooner than 14 days after the splenectomy, but before discharge if she might miss follow-up. Never delay the operation for it.

failures.move: Choosing splenectomy because of the CT grade in a stable patient.
failures.consequence: Removes a spleen that could have been saved, leaving lifelong infection risk.

failures.move: Accepting a negative FAST as excluding injury.
Continuing to observe a patient who has become unstable.
Delaying emergency splenectomy to vaccinate first.
failures.consequence: Postpones haemorrhage control for a measure that belongs after surgery.

recovery.when: You find yourself quoting the grade
recovery.line: The grade informs, but her response to resuscitation decides whether she goes to CT, embolisation or theatre.

recovery.when: Asked about vaccination in an emergency
recovery.line: Never delay the operation: vaccinate afterwards, from 14 days, or before discharge.

knowledge.fact: Stable patients without another indication for laparotomy: non-operative management irrespective of grade.
Non-operative management is contraindicated with unresponsive instability, peritonitis, hollow viscus injury, evisceration or impalement.
Angioembolisation may be first-line for a stable patient with a CT blush irrespective of grade.
In the 2018 AAST scale, any splenic vascular injury or active bleeding makes the injury at least grade IV.
Tranexamic acid as soon as possible; not beyond 3 hours unless hyperfibrinolysis.
Asplenic patients: pneumococcal, meningococcal ACWY and B, annual influenza, and antibiotic prophylaxis (usually phenoxymethylpenicillin).

recall.think: Ongoing splenic bleeding; overwhelming infection after splenectomy.
recall.say: "She is responding, so CT; physiology, not grade, decides."
do: CT if responding; theatre if not

numbers.meaning: no tranexamic acid after this unless hyperfibrinolysis
close observation window in non-operative management

recall.trap: A negative FAST, or a high grade in a stable patient.
recall.finish: Non-operative management with embolisation; laparotomy if unstable or it fails.

sources.name: Coccolini F, et al. Splenic trauma: WSES classification and guidelines for adult and pediatric patients. World J Emerg Surg 2017;12:40
sources.supports: Non-operative management irrespective of grade in stable patients and its facility requirements; contraindications; angioembolisation for blush, pseudoaneurysm and persistent bleeding; operative indications; laparoscopic splenectomy not recommended when bleeding; 48–72 h observation; LMWH once not bleeding; vaccination no sooner than 14 days, or before discharge if likely to be missed

sources.name: NICE guideline NG39: Major trauma: assessment and initial management
sources.supports: Tranexamic acid as soon as possible and not beyond 3 hours unless hyperfibrinolysis (1.5.4–1.5.5); restrictive volume resuscitation (1.5.18); negative FAST does not exclude haemorrhage, immediate CT if responding, FAST not to delay CT (1.5.30–1.5.33)

sources.name: Kozar RA, et al. Organ injury scaling 2018 update: spleen, liver, and kidney. J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2018;85(6):1119–22
sources.supports: Vascular injury or active bleeding classifies a splenic injury as at least grade IV

partner.opening: This young woman has left upper quadrant pain after a bike fall. Pulse 118, BP 96/60. How would you manage her?

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about response to resuscitation
reveals.finding: After 2 units of red cells: pulse 94/min, BP 114/70 mmHg, and holding.
Free fluid in the left upper quadrant and pelvis.
Deep splenic laceration involving hilar vessels with a contrast blush; moderate haemoperitoneum; no other injury.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for repeat bloods at 6 hours
reveals.finding: Haemoglobin 118 g/L on arrival, now 92 g/L; abdomen soft.

push.question: Does the grade decide what you do?
push.expect: No: physiology. Stable with no other laparotomy indication means non-operative management irrespective of grade.

push.question: What would you do about the blush?
When would you operate?
push.expect: Unresponsive instability, peritonitis, or failed non-operative management.

push.question: If she had a splenectomy, when would you vaccinate?
push.expect: No sooner than 14 days, or before discharge; never delay surgery.

curveballs.prompt: Interventional radiology isn't available in this hospital.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Transfer to a centre with it if she is stable; operate if she is not or cannot be transferred safely.

curveballs.prompt: Her blood pressure drops to 80/50 and doesn't respond to blood.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Straight to theatre for laparotomy, not to CT or angiography.
Mechanical prophylaxis now; LMWH may be safe once there is no ongoing bleeding.
